Domain-specific interventions can be necessary. For example, compressing visual-linguistic transformer models faces input misalignment from differing object detectors; adapting the teacher to use the student's region proposals and aligning intermediate tokens enabled effective transfer and marked gains on captioning and VQA benchmarks (Garcia, 2020). This illustrates a general principle: when inputs or tokenization differ, aligning those components substantially improves representational transfer and downstream performance (Garcia, 2020; Potter, 2020).

Limits, failure modes, and open challenges
KD is powerful but not a panacea. Notable failure modes include propagation of teacher errors (especially systematic biases), degradation on rare or long‑tail tokens or classes, sensitivity to distribution shift at deployment, and difficulty aligning heterogeneous architectures without specialized projectors or adaptation steps (Sanders, 2019; Ramos, 2024). Privacy- and communication-constrained settings (federated or on-device learning) require modified KD protocols (data-free or communication-aware variants) and careful evaluation of what behaviors are transferred (Ramos, 2024; Rhodes, 2019). The literature emphasizes that practitioners must test distilled students under the same robustness, fairness, and distribution-shift scenarios expected in deployment rather than relying on in-distribution gains alone (Potter, 2020; Rhodes, 2019).

Best practices and pragmatic recommendations
Synthesis of empirical studies suggests these practical prescriptions: (1) treat KD as part of a compression pipeline and combine it with architecture-aware methods such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search when appropriate (Potter, 2020; Ramos, 2024); (2) select distillation targets to match student capacity—use logits for lightweight transfer, and add intermediate/attention losses when student architecture can support representational alignment (Taylor, 2018; Sanders, 2019); (3) align inputs and tokenization or adapt the teacher when detectors or tokenizers differ (Garcia, 2020); (4) design data strategies—augmentation, selective sampling, or synthetic generation—to match deployment constraints and to reduce harmful teacher–student covariance (Wood, 2021; Ramos, 2024); and (5) evaluate distilled models on long‑tail, robustness, and fairness axes, and iterate teacher or distillation choices accordingly (Potter, 2020; Rhodes, 2019).

Conclusion and research directions
KD has evolved into a rich, practical set of techniques that enable deployable, efficient models across vision and NLP when thoughtfully applied. Future work called for in the literature includes principled methods for heterogeneous teacher–student alignment, better data-free and privacy-preserving distillation, automated selection of which signals to distill for a given student and task, and stronger guarantees under distribution shift and long‑tail behavior (Ramos, 2024; Sanders, 2019). Following the current synthesis—combine appropriate distillation targets, align architectures and inputs, design data strategies deliberately, and integrate KD into a broader compression pipeline—yields the best chances of producing compact models that retain the teacher's useful behavior without amplifying its failures (Taylor, 2018; Potter, 2020).

author: Key
title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted set of techniques for transferring information from large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient student models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, and resource constraints. KD encompasses multiple transfer targets (softened outputs, intermediate features, attention or relational signals), training regimes (offline, online, multi‑teacher) and data strategies (using original data, augmented/synthetic data, or data‑free approaches). In practice KD is most effective when integrated into a compression pipeline that includes architecture-aware design, complementary methods (pruning, quantization), and careful handling of data and teacher–student alignment; however, important limits remain around data scarcity, robustness to distribution shift, and unintended transfer of biases or rare-token behavior.
body:
Definition and scope: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large teacher models into smaller students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone—ranging from softened teacher logits to internal features, attention maps, and relational or contrastive signals. This family of methods operates across modalities (vision, speech, NLP) and under diverse deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy) (Daniel, 2017; Miller, 2019).

What is transferred and why: KD methods differ principally in their transfer targets and objectives. Classic logit/soft-target matching conveys class-probability structure, while feature- or attention-level matching seeks to reproduce intermediate representations and relational structure; these different signals often complement one another and can be chosen to match student capacity and task demands (Daniel, 2017; Miller, 2019).

Training regimes and data strategies: Practitioners treat KD as a system-level pipeline rather than a single loss. Common regimes include offline distillation from a pre-trained teacher, online or mutual distillation schedules, and multi-teacher ensembles. Data regimes range from using the original labeled data through heavy augmentation or synthetic data to fully data-free protocols; choosing a data strategy is critical when original training data are scarce or sensitive (Travis, 2020; Decker, 2023; Cook, 2022).

Complementary compression techniques: KD is frequently combined with structural and numeric compression—pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware search—to achieve deployment targets. Co-designing student architectures, distillation objectives, and complementary methods produces more reliable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs than applying KD alone (Miller, 2019; Cook, 2022).

Empirical outcomes and applications: Across tasks KD often enables students to recover a large fraction of teacher performance while significantly reducing inference cost and memory, making it a practical first-line strategy for many real-world compression problems. KD has been applied to multilingual and translation-related tasks, where distilled students can approach larger-model performance while using far fewer parameters (Travis, 2020; Decker, 2023; Evans, 2019).

Specialized techniques and low-data regimes: When training data are limited, layer-wise or cross-distillation approaches can mitigate accumulated estimation error and reduce overfitting in the student; for example, cross distillation interweaves teacher and student hidden layers to improve few-shot compression (Rocha, 2019). Feature-mimicking approaches that emphasize reproducing teacher feature directions (rather than magnitudes) have also shown empirical gains over logit-only distillation in some settings (Maldonado, 2021).

Interactions with other training practices: KD can interact non-trivially with other regularizers—evidence shows label smoothing can alter the information contained in teacher logits and thus affect distillation outcomes; empirical analyses clarify when label smoothing degrades or is compatible with KD (Adams, 2022).

Limits, risks, and failure modes: KD’s effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, and data alignment. Notable failure modes include degraded transfer under teacher–student mismatch, loss of rare or fine-grained behaviors (important in language tasks), brittleness under distribution shift, and the risk of transferring undesirable behaviors (bias, privacy leaks). These limits motivate careful protocol design, selective transfer of teacher signals, and targeted evaluation (Galloway, 2021; Cook, 2022; Decker, 2023).

Best-practice recommendations: The literature converges on treating KD as a central, context-aware primitive: (1) choose distilled signals to match student capacity and task needs; (2) combine KD with architecture-aware design and complementary compression; (3) adopt data strategies appropriate to availability and privacy constraints (augmentation, synthetic or data-free methods); and (4) evaluate under realistic distribution shifts and for fairness/privacy risks before deployment (Travis, 2020; Cook, 2022; Decker, 2023).

Open directions: Important research gaps remain in theoretical understanding of which signals transfer best, robust data‑free distillation, preserving low-frequency/rare-token behavior in NLP, principled teacher design, and certifying robustness and privacy of distilled models. Addressing these will require hybrid pipelines that integrate pretraining, distillation objectives, and architecture-aware search alongside rigorous evaluation protocols (Daniel, 2017; Miller, 2019).

Summary: Knowledge distillation is a versatile, empirically supported toolkit for producing compact, deployable models in deep learning and NLP. When used as part of an integrated compression pipeline—with careful attention to teacher/student design, data regimes, and complementary techniques—KD routinely produces favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs, but practitioners must guard against mismatch, data scarcity, robustness issues, and harmful transfer of teacher behavior (Daniel, 2017; Miller, 2019; Evans, 2019; Rocha, 2019; Travis, 2020; Galloway, 2021; Maldonado, 2021; Adams, 2022; Cook, 2022; Decker, 2023).

author: Jones
title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical, multi-faceted approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, graph, and other modalities. KD transfers richer supervision than hard labels alone—soft logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, relational signals, and contrastive objectives—often combined with complementary structural compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies. Empirical work shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but success depends on careful teacher–student co-design, choice of distilled signals and objectives, availability and provenance of data, and evaluation for robustness, rare-token behavior, and fairness. Remaining challenges include optimization limits that prevent perfect teacher matching, reliable distillation without original data, protecting against transfer of harmful biases, and principled methods for heterogeneous teacher–student pairs and domain shift.
body:
Overview and framing
Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a broad design pattern for model compression in which richer supervision from a large or ensemble teacher is used to train a smaller student that meets deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy). Multiple recent surveys frame KD as a central, practical element of compression pipelines and emphasize its versatility across modalities and tasks (Contreras, 2017; Cohen, 2021; Nolan, 2022; Horton, 2023). (Contreras, 2017) (Cohen, 2021) (Nolan, 2022) (Horton, 2023)

What is transferred and common objectives
KD methods vary by the form of teacher information transferred. The canonical forms are softened output (logit) matching, intermediate feature or attention-map imitation, relational or pairwise signals, and contrastive or representation-alignment objectives. Surveys and syntheses stress that these signal choices determine what inductive biases and task-relevant information are preserved in the student (Cohen, 2021; Nolan, 2022). (Cohen, 2021) (Nolan, 2022)

- Logit/soft-target matching provides smooth supervision that often improves calibration and generalization relative to hard labels alone (Contreras, 2017; Cohen, 2021). (Contreras, 2017) (Cohen, 2021)
- Feature- and attention-level objectives guide internal representations and can be essential for tasks that rely on structured intermediate computations (Nolan, 2022; Horton, 2023). (Nolan, 2022) (Horton, 2023)
- Relational and contrastive objectives explicitly preserve pairwise or global geometry of teacher representations; these have proven particularly effective for structured domains such as graphs (Ellis, 2020). (Ellis, 2020)

Practical strategies and pipelines
Practitioners typically treat KD as one core element in an integrated compression pipeline that also includes architectural choices, progressive module replacement, pruning, quantization, and data strategies (pretraining, augmentation, synthetic-data or data-free approaches). Multiple syntheses argue that co-design of teacher and student, careful selection of distillation signals, and complementary compression methods are required for reliable deployment (Contreras, 2017; Nolan, 2022; Horton, 2023). (Contreras, 2017) (Nolan, 2022) (Horton, 2023)

- Pre-training compact students before distillation can substantially improve downstream performance and simplify distillation, making "pre-trained distillation" a strong practical baseline for NLP applications (Cameron, 2021). (Cameron, 2021)
- Multi-teacher, online, and collaborative teaching schemes—where temporary or auxiliary teachers guide intermediate stages—can help students follow effective optimization paths and capture diverse teacher knowledge (Gonzalez, 2017). (Gonzalez, 2017)

Empirical evidence and task-specific results
Empirical studies show KD often preserves much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, but outcomes vary by task, data, and signal choice. For example, in reading comprehension an ensemble-to-single distillation with attention-guided answer penalties produced a student with only a 0.4% F1 drop on SQuAD versus an ensemble teacher while running ~12x faster and improving robustness on adversarial sets (Dudley, 2021). (Dudley, 2021)

Domain- and architecture-specific methods have also shown gains. For graph neural networks, contrastive representation distillation that preserves global topology outperforms local-structure-preserving losses across heterogeneous GNNs and large-scale benchmarks (Ellis, 2020). (Ellis, 2020)

For object detection, careful feature imitation using relational metrics (Pearson correlation) mitigates magnitude mismatch and noisy gradients when distilling heterogeneous detectors, yielding consistent mAP improvements (Hahn, 2019). (Hahn, 2019)

Mechanisms, limitations, and open challenges
Despite widespread success, KD is not a panacea. Analyses find substantial optimization barriers and persistent discrepancies between teacher and student predictive distributions even when the student has sufficient capacity; closer matching of teacher outputs does not always translate to better generalization (Arnold, 2017). (Arnold, 2017)

Key practical limitations documented in syntheses include:
- Teacher–student capacity mismatch and layer mapping challenges that complicate which signals are useful and how to align them (Contreras, 2017; Nolan, 2022). (Contreras, 2017) (Nolan, 2022)
- Dependence on data: distillation quality can degrade when original training data are unavailable, which motivates data-free or synthetic-data approaches but raises new robustness and privacy questions (Cohen, 2021; Horton, 2023). (Cohen, 2021) (Horton, 2023)
- Transfer of undesirable behaviors: biases, calibration errors, or adversarial vulnerabilities of teachers can be passed to students unless explicitly mitigated (Cohen, 2021; Nolan, 2022). (Cohen, 2021) (Nolan, 2022)

Design recommendations and best practices
Synthesis works and practical surveys converge on several recommendations:
- Treat KD as a central but not solitary tool: combine it with architecture-aware design, pruning, quantization, and appropriate data strategies (Contreras, 2017; Nolan, 2022; Horton, 2023). (Contreras, 2017) (Nolan, 2022) (Horton, 2023)
- Match distilled signals to student capacity and task needs: use logits for global behavior and feature/attention objectives for tasks requiring internal structure (Cohen, 2021; Nolan, 2022). (Cohen, 2021) (Nolan, 2022)
- Leverage pre-training of compact architectures before distillation in NLP to achieve strong baselines and compound gains (Cameron, 2021). (Cameron, 2021)
- When teachers are ensembles or heterogeneous, consider collaborative/multi-teacher schedules or representation-level objectives that focus on relational information to avoid magnitude-driven noise (Gonzalez, 2017; Hahn, 2019). (Gonzalez, 2017) (Hahn, 2019)

Concluding outlook
KD is an effective, flexible strategy for producing compact models when integrated with thoughtful student architecture design, appropriate distillation signals, and complementary compression methods. Empirical successes across reading comprehension, graph learning, and detection highlight KD’s practical value, while analytical work cautions about optimization limits and data dependencies. Addressing reliable data-free distillation, principled teacher design, mitigating bias transfer, and theoretical understanding of when specific distillation objectives succeed remain important research directions (Contreras, 2017; Cohen, 2021; Nolan, 2022; Horton, 2023; Arnold, 2017). (Contreras, 2017) (Cohen, 2021) (Nolan, 2022) (Horton, 2023) (Arnold, 2017)

author: Morgan
title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring useful behavior from large teacher models into smaller student models so the students can be deployed under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention maps, and relational structure), are implemented in a variety of training regimes (offline teacher-to-student, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, and multi-teacher schedules), and are routinely combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture redesign, and data synthesis). Empirical evidence shows well-designed distillation pipelines often preserve much of a teacher’s performance while delivering substantial gains in efficiency, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data access and provenance, and choices about which signals to transfer. Important open problems include reliable distillation without original data, preserving rare or domain-specific behaviors (especially in NLP), aligning heterogeneous architectures, and maintaining robustness, fairness, and privacy under compression.
body:
Overview and mechanisms: Knowledge distillation is best understood as a family of transfer mechanisms that provide richer supervision than hard labels alone. Common signals include softened output distributions (logits), intermediate feature or attention alignment, relational or correlation-based objectives, and layer-wise or projector-assisted mappings; these different signals accommodate varied teacher–student mismatches and task requirements (Mathis, 2019; Daniels, 2018; Aguirre, 2020). Practical recipes often mix multiple signals (for example logits plus feature matching) to capture both predictive behavior and internal representations (Mathis, 2019; Aguirre, 2020).

Training regimes and schedules: Distillation can be executed in several regimes: offline (pretrained teacher fixed), online or co-distillation (peer teachers/students learn jointly), self-distillation (student re-teaches itself), and multi-teacher/ensemble-to-single transfer. Protocol choices (e.g., teacher annealing or gradual transition from distillation to supervised loss) materially affect multi-task or multi-domain outcomes and can help students exceed their single-task teachers in practice (Ramos, 2022; Perez, 2022).

Integration with other compression primitives: KD is typically a core element of a broader compression pipeline rather than a stand-alone cure. Combining distillation with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or architecture-aware adapters (projectors, layer mapping) yields the best trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and memory for deployment scenarios (Bender, 2020; Aguirre, 2020; Ramos, 2022). Empirical work shows that when student architectures are co-designed with the distillation objective, students reach stronger efficiency–accuracy points than when architectures are chosen ad hoc (Bender, 2020; Frost, 2023).

Applications and modality-specific notes: KD has been applied across vision, language, speech, multimodal, and generative settings. For generative models, compressing GANs via distillation can achieve very high compression ratios while retaining sample quality on benchmark datasets, although qualitative limits and task-specific constraints appear (e.g., a compression ceiling for particular generators) (Herrera, 2018). In NLP, approaches such as progressive module replacement (the BERT-of-Theseus style) and distillation variants tailored to transformer modules provide alternative or complementary pathways to standard logit-based KD (Gray, 2019).

Practical determinants of success: Several consistent factors govern distillation outcomes: teacher quality and specialization (higher-quality or well-matched teachers generally produce better students), student capacity and architecture (insufficient capacity limits what can be recovered), and data availability and provenance (access to representative task data improves transfer). When those conditions are favorable, distilled students can approach teacher performance with much lower cost; when they are not, targeted design choices (signal selection, projectors, synthetic data) are necessary to avoid large degradations (Frost, 2023; Mathis, 2019; Ramos, 2022).

Data-limited, data-free, and privacy-aware regimes: When original training data are unavailable, practitioners rely on synthetic-data generation, data-free distillation protocols, or privacy-aware distributed/federated distillation. These approaches extend KD’s applicability but introduce new risks and trade-offs—synthetic samples may not cover rare or domain-specific phenomena and privacy-aware aggregation can limit the richness of transferable signals (Ramos, 2022; Aguirre, 2020).

Robustness, fairness, and long-tail behavior: Distillation can propagate undesirable teacher behaviors (biases, overconfidence, or brittleness) into students if not explicitly mitigated, and preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors in NLP remains difficult under heavy compression. Targeted objectives—such as fairness-aware feature distillation—have been proposed to reduce algorithmic bias while retaining accuracy, showing that distillation can be adapted to mitigate, not only transmit, certain harms (Roman, 2020). Still, systematic evaluation under distribution shift and safety-critical metrics is an ongoing need (Frost, 2023; Bender, 2020).

Alternative and complementary design patterns: Beyond classic loss-based KD, practitioners have shown success with architectural replacement schedules (progressive module replacing), born‑again or teacher-annealing strategies for multi-task transfer, and meta-learned or multi-teacher curricula that shape what students learn across tasks and domains (Gray, 2019; Perez, 2022; Ramos, 2022). These patterns illustrate that distillation is as much a system-level design choice as a loss-term addition.

Open challenges and research directions: Key open problems include: (1) principled mapping of which signals to transfer for heterogeneous teachers and students; (2) reliable data-free or privacy-preserving distillation that preserves rare, safety-critical, or minority-class behaviors; (3) reducing the computation and emissions cost of distillation itself while maintaining fidelity; and (4) stronger theoretical understanding of when distillation improves student generalization versus when it simply transfers teacher idiosyncrasies (Mathis, 2019; Frost, 2023; Aguirre, 2020).

Summary guidance for practitioners: Treat KD as a core, system-level primitive that must be co-designed with student architecture and deployment constraints. Select distilled signals to match student capacity, combine distillation with complementary compression steps (pruning, quantization, architecture search), and if operating without original data or under privacy constraints, plan for synthetic-data or federated-distillation workflows and robust evaluation of rare-class and fairness metrics (Ramos, 2022; Bender, 2020; Aguirre, 2020). When applied with these considerations, KD provides a flexible, empirically validated route to compact, high-quality models across deep learning modalities (Mathis, 2019; Daniels, 2018; Frost, 2023).

author: Roberts
title: Knowledge Distillation as a First‑Line, Context‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible toolkit for converting large teacher models into smaller, deployable students that preserve much of task performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute. KD supports multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), training regimes (offline, online, multi‑teacher), and data strategies (real, augmented, synthetic, and data‑free), and it integrates naturally with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture co‑design. Treated as a default first‑line strategy, KD should be applied with explicit attention to teacher–student co‑design, data provenance, and evaluation for robustness, fairness, and rare‑token behaviors; where those safeguards are impractical, alternative or complementary compression steps are required. This paper argues that KD be adopted as the standard initial approach for model compression in deep learning and NLP, while documenting its typical failure modes and practical mitigations.
body:
Position summary: Knowledge distillation should be treated as the default, first‑line strategy for model compression in deep learning and NLP when the goal is to deliver compact, high‑quality models for deployment. This recommendation rests on three pillars: (1) consistent empirical gains across tasks and modalities, (2) methodological breadth that adapts to practical constraints, and (3) compatibility with complementary compression methods—combined with clear, manageable failure modes that require explicit engineering controls.

Empirical effectiveness across tasks and modalities: A large body of reviews and empirical work shows KD routinely recovers much of a teacher’s performance while substantially reducing inference costs across language, vision, and other domains (Warner, 2021; Liu, 2024; Dudley, 2023). These syntheses report repeated successes in pre‑trained language models, retrieval and ranking, visual recognition, and resource‑constrained edge scenarios, supporting the practical claim that KD provides strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs in real deployments (Warner, 2021; Liu, 2024).

Methodological diversity and adaptability: KD is not a single loss term but a toolkit: soft‑label (logit) matching, intermediate‑feature or attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, multi‑teacher and online schedules, and data‑free synthesis are all viable options depending on constraints (Calderon, 2017; Andrews, 2020; Fisher, 2024). That diversity means practitioners can select or combine signals that best match student capacity, architecture mismatch, and the available data budget—making KD broadly applicable in heterogeneous production settings (Calderon, 2017; Andrews, 2020).

Practical integration with other compression primitives: KD complements pruning, quantization, and architecture search rather than displacing them. Combining KD with these techniques yields compact models that meet tight latency and memory budgets while retaining representational quality; multiple surveys emphasize KD’s role as a system‑level choice within broader compression pipelines (Fisher, 2024; Torres, 2024). In practice, using KD first to transfer predictive behavior and representations, then applying pruning or quantization as fine‑grained efficiency steps, produces reliable end results (Fisher, 2024).

Addressing data and privacy constraints: KD adapts to limited or sensitive data through approaches such as data augmentation, synthetic‑data distillation, and data‑free methods that synthesize inputs to elicit teacher behavior (Calderon, 2017; Torres, 2024). These variations make KD suitable for privacy‑aware or federated deployments where raw training data cannot be shared, broadening its applicability as a first‑line method under real‑world constraints (Calderon, 2017; Torres, 2024).

Failure modes and necessary safeguards: Although broadly effective, KD has documented failure modes that argue for a context‑aware default rather than an unconditional prescription. Key risks include propagation of teacher errors or undesirable biases, optimization mismatch between teacher and compact student capacities, and degraded behavior under distribution shift or for rare tokens/labels (Warner, 2021; Andrews, 2020; Fisher, 2024). These reviews recommend explicit safeguards—teacher quality control, mixing hard labels with distilled soft targets, curriculum or layer‑mapping strategies, and evaluation on edge cases—to avoid transferring harmful or brittle behaviors (Warner, 2021; Andrews, 2020).

Practical guidelines for first‑line use: Based on the convergent recommendations in the literature, adopt the following workflow when using KD as your first step:
- Start with a high‑quality teacher and validate its behavior on safety‑ and fairness‑critical slices before distillation (Warner, 2021; Arnold, 2022).
- Choose distillation signals to match student capacity: logits for lightweight students, intermediate/attention matches for richer representational transfer (Calderon, 2017; Andrews, 2020).
- When data are limited or private, use synthetic or data‑free distillation techniques and augment with task‑aware sampling (Calderon, 2017; Torres, 2024).
- Integrate KD with pruning/quantization/architecture search as follow‑on steps rather than replacements; verify performance and robustness after each compression stage (Fisher, 2024; Torres, 2024).
- Monitor failure modes (teacher biases, rare‑token loss, distribution shift) and apply mitigations such as multi‑teacher ensembling, teacher confidence weighting, or mixing hard labels to stabilize training (Warner, 2021; Arnold, 2022).

Conclusion: The literature supports treating knowledge distillation as the standard first‑line strategy for model compression in deep learning and NLP because it consistently delivers strong tradeoffs, adapts to varied constraints, and composes well with other compression methods (Warner, 2021; Liu, 2024; Dudley, 2023; Calderon, 2017; Andrews, 2020; Fisher, 2024; Arnold, 2022; Torres, 2024). That recommendation comes with an important caveat: KD should be used as a context‑aware toolkit—accompanied by teacher validation, careful signal selection, data strategies, and post‑distillation robustness checks—to avoid well‑known failure modes and to ensure safe, reliable deployment.
